slides.title: ChipStain
slides.subtitle: Label-free nuclear staining that tells you where not to trust it
bullets: Team Hack2Publish — Md. Hamid Hosen, Esfer Sami, Foysal
slides.narration: We are team Hack2Publish — Hamid, Esfer and Foysal — and this is ChipStain, in the Model and Algorithm category.

slides.title: Nuclear read-outs need a stain — and a stain has a cost
bullets: Cell number, growth and viability on an organ-on-a-chip all start from a nuclear stain
Fixation ends the experiment; live DNA dyes are phototoxic
Reporter lines are rarely available for iPSC-derived tissue such as neurons
In-silico labeling predicts the stain — but a point prediction gives no warning when it is wrong
slides.narration: Almost every read-out on an organ-on-a-chip — cell number, growth, viability — starts from a nuclear stain. But fixation ends the experiment, live DNA dyes are phototoxic, and reporter lines are rarely available for iPSC-derived tissue such as neurons. In-silico labeling can predict the stain from a bright-field image, but a plain prediction gives no warning when it is wrong.

slides.title: Predict the stain and its uncertainty
bullets: U-Net, ImageNet ResNet-34 encoder; head predicts mean μ and variance σ² per pixel
β-NLL loss keeps the variance from swallowing hard pixels
8× test-time augmentation: σ² = learned variance + TTA disagreement
No new mechanism — the contribution is testing whether σ actually helps
slides.narration: ChipStain is a U-Net whose head predicts, for every pixel, a mean and a variance, trained with the beta N L L loss. At test time we average eight flipped and rotated views; their disagreement is added to the learned variance. Nothing here is a new mechanism. What we contribute is testing whether this uncertainty actually helps, against honest baselines.

slides.title: {{n_demo_count}} nuclei found — the reference has {{n_demo_ref}}
bullets: Bright-field in → predicted H2B and σ out, on a laptop CPU
σ is higher on nuclei and near zero on background
Mean σ = {{n_demo_sigma_clean}}
slides.narration: Here is a bright-field image from a well the model never saw. On a laptop CPU we get the predicted nuclear stain and the uncertainty map. Sigma is higher on nuclei — brighter means noisier — and near zero on background. The app counts {{n_demo_count}} nuclei; the dataset's reference annotation has {{n_demo_ref}}.

slides.kicker: Demo · same image, blurred by 1 px
slides.title: The prediction fails — and σ says so
bullets: Mean σ jumps from {{n_demo_sigma_clean}} to {{n_demo_sigma_blur}}
The app warns: input looks unlike the training data
A plain U-Net becomes less uncertain here — it fails silently
slides.narration: Now the same image, slightly blurred — a crude stand-in for defocus. The prediction falls apart, and the uncertainty jumps from {{n_demo_sigma_clean}} to {{n_demo_sigma_blur}}; the app warns that the input looks unlike its training data. A plain U-Net in this situation becomes less uncertain — it fails silently.

slides.title: Same fidelity, much better uncertainty
slides.narration: Over three training runs on 125 test images, ChipStain matches a U-Net with the same augmentation in correlation with the real stain — {{n_full_pearson}} versus {{n_bt_pearson}} — at a {{n_mae_rel}} percent higher pixel error. Its uncertainty ranks errors clearly better — Spearman {{n_full_rho}} versus {{n_bt_rho}}, in every test field and every seed — and it is close to calibrated: the 95 percent interval covers {{n_cal_95}} percent of pixels.

slides.title: When the input drifts, σ rises — the baseline's falls
bullets: Blur and phase-contrast input break both models' predictions
ChipStain's mean σ rises several-fold and flags the failed images
The U-Net's TTA spread falls under blur
slides.narration: We stressed both models with blur, noise and a different imaging modality. Both predictions break, ChipStain's more. But its uncertainty rises several-fold and flags the failed images, while the baseline's uncertainty falls — it fails silently.

slides.title: 60 hours of growth from bright-field alone
slides.narration: On a 60-hour time-lapse, counting nuclei on the prediction gives a doubling time of {{n_tl_dt_pred}} hours, against {{n_tl_dt_real}} from the real stain. And an uncertainty gate fixed on validation data cuts the doubling-time error across training runs from {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} percent.

slides.title: What σ does not do
bullets: For counting alone, direct segmentation wins: Cellpose F1 {{n_cp_f1}} vs ours {{n_full_segf1}}
Per-nucleus σ is no better than a simple brightness rule
No organ-on-chip images were available — validation is in a plate and a dish
{{neural_slide}}
slides.narration: To be clear about the limits: if you only need a nuclear count, a segmentation model trained on matching labels does better — Cellpose reaches F1 {{n_cp_f1}} versus our {{n_full_segf1}}. Per-nucleus sigma is no better than a simple brightness rule. And we had no organ-on-chip images. {{neural_video}}
